title: How he compiled
hook: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi, side by side with the Gurus: how Guru Arjan chose what went into the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan sang that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other, and serves the One alone. Your line was serving the one. Whom did you serve with your whole attention? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

A stack of handwritten pages, gathered from many hands. Some hold the Gurus' hymns, copied and recopied in different towns, a word drifting here and there. Some hold songs by saints who were never Gurus at all: a weaver, a man who worked with hides, a Sufi from the Punjab. And tradition says some of the pages going around carried the Guru's name without the Guru's voice. Somebody has to sit with all of it and decide what goes into one book, and what stays out. Today, Guru Arjan is the editor.
screen: `A STACK OF PAGES, MANY HANDS.` → `SAINTS WHO WERE NEVER GURUS.` → `WHAT GOES IN, WHAT STAYS OUT?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and dictated the volume to Bhai Gurdas, who wrote it out. The book became the Adi Granth, which later became the Guru Granth Sahib. So what was his test? Not where a singer was born. Not which faith he grew up in. Not whether his trade was respected. The test was whether the hymn agreed with the Guru's teaching: the One, the Name, the turning away from ego. Look at who passed. Kabir calls himself a weaver, right there in his own verses. Ravidas names his people's work with hides and dead cattle, work his society looked down on, and sings that the learned now bow to him because of the Name. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, has his saloks near the end of the Granth. These aren't footnotes at the back. They're sung in the gurdwara, in the same ragas as the Gurus' hymns. One more detail sits on the page itself. Among Farid's saloks, a few verses are marked Mahala three and Mahala five: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, answering. Where one of Farid's lines could be heard too harshly, a Guru's line sits beside it, turning it a little. So choosing carefully meant two things at once. A wide welcome, and a real conversation. The Guru didn't flatten the voices into one. He let them sing, and he answered. And the question travels, because each of us compiles something. The feed you scroll, the voices you let into your head at night, the friend whose advice you keep. Guru Arjan's question isn't, is this person like me? It's, does this agree with the truth I'm trying to live?
screen: `THE GURU DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `THE TEST: DOES IT AGREE?` · `A WEAVER, A LEATHERWORKER, A SUFI.` · `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID.` · then, large: `HE CHOSE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one good voice to keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the voices of your week pass by: a podcast, a parent, a teacher, a song, a friend's text. Don't judge them yet. Just let them come. Now ask the editor's question of each one: does this agree with the person I'm trying to become? One voice will stand out. Maybe a surprising one, from somewhere you didn't expect. Keep it. Hold one thing it said, and let it sit with you. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
How he compiled. Guru Arjan gathered many voices, Gurus and saints, and kept the ones that agreed with the Guru's teaching, whoever sang them. Today's word.
Your line: he chose carefully. Today, before you share, forward or repeat something, ask the editor's question once: does it agree with what I'm trying to live? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, the hymns of the Gurus and of the bhagats, such as Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid, are read and sung from the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bow to the whole as the Guru.

fork.setup: you're compiling a holy book. a song by a weaver from another tradition agrees with everything your Guru taught. what do you do?
options: leave it out: he isn't one of the Gurus.
put it in, and sing it with the Gurus' hymns.
keep it in a separate book of extras.
fork.reveal: Guru Arjan put the bhagats' hymns in the same book, sung in the same ragas. what counted was whether a hymn agreed with the teaching.

original.note: the Word, the hymns; Sikhs speak of gurbani, the Guru's word, and of bhagat bani, the saints' hymns in the Granth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru collected his favorite songs.
what it means: he chose hymns that agreed with the Guru's teaching, from Gurus and from saints of other backgrounds.
what a scholar hears: among Farid's saloks sit verses marked Mahala three and five, the Gurus answering a saint inside the book itself.
